module_title: Basic Tissue Converting: From Jumbo Roll to Finished Product

lessons.title: How a Toilet Roll Rewinding Machine Works
lessons.body: A toilet roll rewinding machine takes a large jumbo roll of tissue paper (typically 2.5 to 3 meters wide) and converts it into smaller, finished rolls. The machine has several key parts: a jumbo roll stand, a web tension control system, a perforation unit, a rewinding mandrel, and a log saw. First, you load the jumbo roll onto the stand. The tissue paper is threaded through a series of rollers that maintain tension. Too much tension tears the paper; too little causes wrinkles. Next, the paper passes through the perforation unit, which has a rotating blade that cuts small slits at regular intervalsâusually every 12 to 15 centimeters. This allows you to tear off sheets easily. Then the paper is wound onto a cardboard core (the inner tube) on the rewinding mandrel. The machine counts the number of sheets per roll (common counts: 200, 300, 500) and stops when the log reaches the desired diameter. The finished log is ejected, and a new core is inserted automatically or manually. Finally, the log moves to a log saw, which cuts it into individual rolls of standard widthâtypically 10 to 12 centimeters. In small African workshops, manual or semi-automatic rewinders are common. They cost less but require an operator to feed cores and monitor tension. A basic manual rewinder can produce 100 to 200 rolls per hour, while a semi-automatic one can do 500 to 800. The key is to keep the jumbo roll centered, adjust the perforation blade sharpness, and maintain consistent winding speed. With practice, you can produce quality rolls that compete with imported brands.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Small-Scale Converting Line in Your Workshop
lessons.body: To start a small-scale tissue converting line, you need a space of at least 6 by 8 meters with a smooth concrete floor, good lighting, and ventilation. Your main equipment: a jumbo roll stand (can be locally welded), a rewinding machine (manual or semi-automatic), a log saw (circular saw with a jig), a core cutter, and a sealing machine for wrapping. You also need a supply of jumbo rolls (from a paper mill), cardboard cores (2.5 cm inner diameter), and plastic wrap. Arrange the line in a U-shape: jumbo roll at one end, rewinder in the middle, log saw and wrapping table at the other end. This reduces walking and increases flow. Power requirements: a semi-automatic rewinder needs 1.5 to 2.2 kW, a log saw 1.1 kW. If you have unstable electricity, invest in a 5 kVA generator or inverter. Water is not needed except for cleaning. For safety, install guards on all rotating parts and provide dust masksâtissue dust is a respiratory irritant. Start with a manual rewinder (cost: $800â$1,500) and upgrade as you grow. You can build a simple log saw using a circular saw mounted on a table with a sliding carriage. For cores, buy pre-cut or cut your own from long tubes using a core cutter. A good layout allows two workers to produce 300â500 rolls per day. Keep raw materials dryâmoisture causes jumbo rolls to stick and tear. Label your finished products with your brand, roll count, and ply. Many successful African converters start in a garage or small room and expand gradually.

lessons.title: Adjusting Tension and Perforation for Quality Rolls
lessons.body: Tension and perforation are the two most critical adjustments for quality toilet rolls. Tension controls how tightly the paper is wound. If tension is too high, the roll becomes hard, the paper stretches and may tear during unwinding, and the perforations break prematurely. If tension is too low, the roll is loose, feels cheap, and may telescope (the inner layers slip out). To set tension, start with the jumbo roll brake or dancer roller. On a manual rewinder, you adjust a friction brake on the jumbo roll stand. Turn the knob until the paper feels taut but still flexibleâyou should be able to press a finger into the roll and feel slight give. A simple test: pull a sheet; it should resist but not snap. For perforation, the blade must be sharp and set at the correct angle. Dull blades cause torn perforationsâragged edges that make the roll hard to tear. Set the perforation length to 12â15 cm (about 5â6 inches). You can adjust the perforation unit by rotating the blade holder or changing gears. The blade should cut through about 80% of the paper thickness, leaving a small uncut portion to hold the log together during winding. Test by tearing a sheet: it should separate cleanly with a straight edge. If it tears diagonally or leaves fuzz, adjust blade depth or replace the blade. Also check perforation alignmentâthe cut should be perpendicular to the paper edge. In humid conditions, paper absorbs moisture and becomes weaker, so reduce tension slightly. In dry conditions, increase tension a bit. Regularly clean the perforation blade with a soft brush to remove paper dust. With practice, you'll learn to feel the right tension and hear the right perforation soundâa crisp 'snick' means good cutting.

lessons.title: Cutting Logs into Rolls: Manual and Semi-Automatic Methods
lessons.body: After rewinding, you have a long log of tissueâoften 1.5 to 2 meters long. You must cut it into individual rolls of 10â12 cm width. Manual cutting uses a hand saw or a miter box. For small production, a simple jig: a wooden V-block that holds the log, and a fine-tooth hand saw (24 teeth per inch). Mark the log with a measuring tape and pencil every 10 cm. Cut with smooth, even strokesâdon't force the saw, or you'll crush the roll. This method yields 50â80 rolls per hour but is tiring and less accurate. Semi-automatic cutting uses a circular saw mounted on a table with a sliding carriage. You clamp the log in a holder, then push the carriage through the saw blade. A stop block sets the cut length. This is faster (200â400 rolls per hour) and more consistent. Safety: wear gloves and safety glasses; keep hands away from the blade. For either method, use a sharp blade designed for paperâa dull blade tears the tissue and creates dust. After cutting, inspect each roll: edges should be clean, not fuzzy. If edges are torn, your blade is dull or the log was wound too loosely. You can also use a bandsaw for smoother cuts, but it's more expensive. In many African workshops, a converted woodworking circular saw works well. Set the blade height to just above the log diameter. Feed the log slowly to avoid burning. After cutting, tap the rolls gently to align the layers. Store cut rolls in a dry placeâhumidity makes them swell and jam in wrapping machines. For higher output, consider a fully automatic log saw, but it costs $5,000+. Start manual, then upgrade to semi-automatic when you reach 500 rolls per day.

lessons.title: Wrapping and Sealing Toilet Rolls by Hand or Machine
lessons.body: Wrapping protects the rolls from dust, moisture, and handling damage. It also carries your brand. For hand wrapping, you need a roll of plastic film (typically 20â30 microns thick, either clear or printed), a heat sealer or a simple candle or hot wire, and a roll of tape. Cut a piece of film about 30 cm by 20 cm. Place the roll in the center, fold the film around it, and tuck the ends into the core. Seal the seam with a heat sealer or a hot wireâpress for 1â2 seconds. For a more professional look, use a shrink wrap gun: wrap the roll loosely, then apply heat; the film shrinks tight. Hand wrapping produces 100â200 rolls per hour. Machine wrapping uses a flow wrapper or a shrink tunnel. A semi-automatic wrapping machine (cost: $1,500â$3,000) feeds rolls on a conveyor, wraps them in film, and seals with a heated bar. Output: 800â1,200 rolls per hour. For sealing, ensure the temperature is correctâtoo hot burns the film, too cold leaves weak seals. Test by pulling the seam; it should not open. Common mistakes: loose wraps (film not tight enough) and torn film (from sharp edges on the roll). To avoid loose wraps, stretch the film slightly as you wrap. For machine wrapping, adjust the film tension roller. Also, make sure the roll is centered. Use printed film to show your brand, roll count, and ply. In Africa, many small producers use clear film and a simple label sticker. That's fineâjust ensure the label is waterproof. Store wrapped rolls in a cool, dry place away from sunlight, which can degrade the plastic.

lessons.title: Quality Checks: Avoiding Loose Wraps and Torn Perforations
lessons.body: Quality control is what separates a professional operation from a hobby. Two common defects are loose wraps and torn perforations. Loose wraps: the plastic film is not tight, allowing the roll to shift and look sloppy. Causes: insufficient film tension, wrong film thickness (too thin), or sealing temperature too low. Fix: increase film tension on the machine or stretch by hand; use 25â30 micron film; raise sealing temperature by 5â10Â°C. Test: hold the wrapped roll and squeeze gentlyâthe film should not slide. Torn perforations: the perforation line is ragged or breaks when you tear a sheet. Causes: dull perforation blade, wrong blade depth, or too much tension. Fix: replace or sharpen the blade; adjust depth to cut 80% of paper; reduce tension. Test: tear a sheet; it should separate cleanly with a straight line. Other checks: roll diameter (should be consistent, e.g., 10â12 cm), sheet count (verify by counting sheets on a sample roll), and core alignment (core should be centered). Also check for 'telescoping'âinner layers sticking outâwhich means tension was too low. And 'starring'âwrinkles radiating from the coreâcaused by too much tension. Do these checks every 30 minutes: pull a random roll from the line, unwrap it, and inspect. Keep a log of defects and adjustments. Train your workers to spot problems early. In hot, humid African climates, paper absorbs moisture, so adjust tension and perforation daily. A simple checklist: 1) Tear test, 2) Squeeze test, 3) Measure diameter, 4) Count sheets. If you find defects, stop and fix before continuing. Consistent quality builds customer trust and repeat sales.

quiz.q: What is the typical width of a jumbo roll used in toilet roll converting?
quiz.explanation: Jumbo rolls are typically 2.5 to 3 meters wide, allowing multiple rolls to be cut from one log.

quiz.q: What does the perforation unit do on a rewinding machine?
options: A) Cuts the log into rolls
B) Winds the paper onto the core
C) Makes small slits for easy tearing
quiz.explanation: The perforation unit creates small slits at regular intervals so sheets can be torn off easily.

quiz.q: What is a common sheet count for a toilet roll?
quiz.explanation: Common sheet counts include 200, 300, and 500 sheets per roll.

quiz.q: What is the typical width of an individual toilet roll?
quiz.explanation: Finished toilet rolls are usually 10 to 12 centimeters wide.

quiz.q: What is the function of a log saw?
options: B) To cut the log into individual rolls
quiz.explanation: The log saw cuts the long wound log into individual rolls of standard width.

quiz.q: What is a typical production rate for a manual rewinder?
quiz.explanation: A basic manual rewinder can produce 100 to 200 rolls per hour.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended space for a small-scale converting line?
quiz.explanation: A space of at least 6 by 8 meters is recommended for a small-scale converting line.

quiz.q: Why should you arrange the converting line in a U-shape?
options: B) To reduce walking and increase flow
D) To make it look neat
quiz.explanation: A U-shape reduces walking distance and improves material flow.

quiz.q: What power rating is typical for a semi-automatic rewinder?
quiz.explanation: A semi-automatic rewinder typically requires 1.5 to 2.2 kW of power.

quiz.q: What is a safety precaution when operating a log saw?
options: B) Remove guards for better access
C) Wear gloves and safety glasses
D) Use a dull blade to reduce speed
quiz.explanation: Gloves and safety glasses protect against cuts and flying debris.

quiz.q: What happens if tension is too high on the rewinder?
options: A) The roll becomes too loose
B) The paper may tear and perforations break
quiz.explanation: High tension stretches the paper and can cause tearing and premature perforation breakage.

quiz.q: What is a sign of too little tension?
quiz.explanation: Low tension causes the inner layers to slip out, known as telescoping.

quiz.q: What is the recommended perforation length for toilet rolls?
quiz.explanation: Perforations are typically spaced 12 to 15 centimeters apart.

quiz.q: What causes torn perforations?
quiz.explanation: A dull perforation blade causes ragged, torn perforations.

quiz.q: How deep should the perforation blade cut?
quiz.explanation: The blade should cut through about 80% of the paper thickness to hold the log together.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for correct tension?
options: A) Pull a sheet; it should snap immediately
B) Pull a sheet; it should resist but not snap
C) Squeeze the roll; it should be very hard
D) Drop the roll; it should bounce
quiz.explanation: Correct tension allows the paper to resist pulling but not tear easily.

quiz.q: What is a common manual method for cutting logs?
options: B) Hand saw with a miter box
quiz.explanation: A hand saw with a miter box or V-block is a common manual method.

quiz.q: What is a safety tip when using a semi-automatic log saw?
options: A) Keep hands close to the blade
B) Use a dull blade to reduce speed
C) Wear safety glasses and keep hands away
D) Remove the guard for better visibility
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses protect eyes, and keeping hands away prevents cuts.

quiz.q: What is the typical output of a semi-automatic log saw?
quiz.explanation: A semi-automatic log saw can cut 200 to 400 rolls per hour.

quiz.q: Why should cut rolls be stored in a dry place?
options: A) To prevent them from burning
B) To prevent swelling and jamming
quiz.explanation: Humidity causes rolls to swell and can jam wrapping machines.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of plastic film for hand wrapping?
quiz.explanation: Plastic film for hand wrapping is typically 20 to 30 microns thick.

quiz.q: How long should you press a heat sealer for hand wrapping?
quiz.explanation: Pressing for 1 to 2 seconds is usually enough to seal the film.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in wrapping?
quiz.explanation: Loose wraps occur when the film is not tight enough, allowing the roll to shift.

quiz.q: What causes loose wraps?
quiz.explanation: Insufficient film tension results in loose wraps.

quiz.q: What is a quality check for wrapped rolls?
quiz.explanation: A gentle squeeze test checks if the film is tight and does not slide.

quiz.q: What is 'telescoping' in a toilet roll?
options: A) The roll is too hard
C) The roll is too long
quiz.explanation: Telescoping occurs when inner layers slip out due to low tension.

quiz.q: What is 'starring' in a toilet roll?
options: A) Wrinkles radiating from the core
quiz.explanation: Starring refers to wrinkles radiating from the core, caused by too much tension.

quiz.q: How often should you perform quality checks on the production line?
options: D) Only at the end of the shift
quiz.explanation: Checking every 30 minutes helps catch defects early.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a defect?
options: A) Continue production and fix later
B) Stop and fix before continuing
quiz.explanation: Stopping to fix defects prevents more defective products.

quiz.q: Why is consistent quality important?
options: B) It builds customer trust and repeat sales
quiz.explanation: Consistent quality leads to customer satisfaction and repeat business.
